t: after first tithe is separated every year. For first tithe applies in all years (except the Shemittah year).
second tithe is separated. A tenth of what remains.
and in the third and sixth year. According to the Shemittah cycle.
in place of. Instead of.
as we explained. Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 6:1-4.
on the first of Tishrei etc.. See also Hilchot Terumot 5:11.
for the season of tithes. The stage of growth at which produce becomes obligated in terumot and ma'asrot (see Hilchot Ma'aser 2:3-5).
that were completed. Ripened fully.
and were gathered. Were picked.
are tithed as of the past. According to the law of the previous year.
whose fruit has set. That began to ripen (the time of the fruit's setting is "the season of tithes" - Rikkevo, Chazon Ish, Shevi'it 7:12).
carobs of Tzalmonah. Carobs that grow in a place named Tzalmonah.
greens are tithed at the time of their picking. The time of plucking the greens is the determining time for the obligation of tithes.

it is like greens, and one follows its picking. The etrog is treated as a vegetable in this respect, in that the determining time is its picking, but its New Year is on the 15th of Shevat, like the fruit of trees.
whether for tithes. For determining whether it is subject to second tithe or the poor man's tithe.

or for Shemittah. If it was picked in a Shemittah year it has the holiness of Shevi'it (Hilchot Shemittah 4:12; and see there 4:9 that the Shemittah year begins on the first of Tishrei also with regard to the fruit of trees, so that fruit that sets after the first of Tishrei has the holiness of Shevi'it, as do vegetables picked or an etrog picked at that time).

and even though one follows its picking etc.. Although with regard to the holiness of Shevi'it the determining time for an etrog is its picking, nevertheless if it reached the season of tithes in the sixth year it becomes obligated in tithes. And although Shevi'it produce is exempt from tithes (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 6:5), the Sages were stringent and obligated it in tithes like other fruit that set in the sixth year, even if its main growth was in the Shemittah year, for example if in the sixth year it was the size of an olive and in the seventh year it grew to the size of a jar (see also Hilchot Shemittah 4:12).
the avionot of the caper. The caper is a perennial thorny shrub called by this name also today, and the avionot are its fruits.

they apply to them the stringencies of trees and the stringencies of seeds. The determining time for avionot is their picking (like greens). But as for their New Year, the Sages were uncertain whether it is on the first of Tishrei, like greens, or on the 15th of Shevat, like trees.
and afterward he separates another tithe and redeems it. Like second-tithe produce, whose holiness may be transferred to money (as below 4:1).
and after he redeems it, he gives it to the poor. Like poor man's tithe produce.
and he eats its redemption money as second tithe. He buys food with the money and eats it in Jerusalem, according to the law of eating second tithe explained in the following chapters.
rice and millet etc.. See also Hilchot Shemittah 4:11.

the completion of the fruit. Its full ripening; for these species one does not follow the season of tithes as with other legumes, since each bed reaches this stage at a different time (Ribamatz, Shevi'it 2:7, based on Babylonian Talmud Rosh Hashanah 13b, and see there Tosafot s.v. acher).
Egyptian beans. A species of legume found only in Egypt (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nedarim 7:2).

he gathers his grain pile into it. He may gather into one place produce that took root this year and produce that took root last year (and see further below halachah 10 for more details about the laws of Egyptian beans).

the sterile onions. A species of onion that requires abundant irrigation, called "saris" (sterile, that does not produce seed) because it is unlike other onions, which sprout and put out leaves when placed in a damp place after being uprooted from the ground (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 2:9, and see also Hilchot Shemittah 4:17).
and of the ba'al. Ordinary onions that live mostly on rainwater.

that he withheld from them three seasons. Three irrigation times; the fact that he withheld water from these species shows that they have reached full ripening and are about to be plucked from the ground (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).

are tithed as of the past. Tithe is separated from them according to the law of the year that is ending, as they are judged as if they were plucked, and for vegetables one follows the year of picking (Rikkevo).

he tithes from its seed on its greens and from its greens on its seed. The seeds and the pods are tithed together, and one follows the completion of the fruit, as with one who sows without specification.

its seed is tithed as of the past... provided that he picked from it before Rosh Hashanah. When he picked from the seeds before Rosh Hashanah, the seeds are judged by the passing year even if they did not reach a third of their growth, for they will never reach a third.
and its greens at the time of its picking. If there are fresh pods that he wishes to eat as greens, they are judged separately and one follows the time of picking.
and he intended it for greens. After sowing he changed his mind and decided that he wants it for greens.
one follows his intention. According to his latest intention, and it is judged as greens.
the intention of seed does not apply to it. His latest intention has no power to cancel his first intention.

unless he withheld from it three arayot. He did not pick from it at three picking times, as is done with Egyptian beans sown for seed, which are not picked but one waits for the seeds to dry. For when he does an act that shows that he now wants it for seed, this has the power to cancel his first intention.
arayot. Pickings.

but if it brought etc.. When it brought a third after Rosh Hashanah, there is no distinction between one who sows for seed and one who sows for greens, and so it is tithed according to the new year even if he did not do an act showing his change of mind.

he sowed it for seed etc.. This case branches from the case in the previous paragraph, where he sowed for seed and afterward intended it for greens; but in this case he waited until the pods fully ripened and began to dry ("completed ketzatzim"), from which it is apparent that he wants to eat the dry seeds, as in his first intention.
and its greens at the time of its picking. If additional pods grew, they are judged by his second intention.

part of it made completed ketzatzim etc.. In this case it appears that he wants both seed, as in his first intention, and greens, as in his second intention, and so the seeds and the pods are tithed together, and one follows the completion of the fruit, as with a person whose intention is not clear.

this is what we said. Above, halachah 8. In understanding the various details of this halachah and its relation to halachah 8 there are many difficulties, and the commentators took different paths (see for example Rikkevo and Derekh Emunah), and we have explained it according to Aruch HaShulchan, Zera'im 118:24-30, with added explanation from the commentary of R. Y. Felix on Jerusalem Talmud Shevi'it 2:5.
if he sowed it for seed. For eating the dry kernels (Rashi, Rosh Hashanah 13b; and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 2:8, Hamaor edition and the note there).

it is tithed as of the past. For in this case the determining time for tithes is a third of its growth, like grain (see Hilchot Ma'aser 2:5). And above in halachah 8 it speaks of one who sowed the beans without any particular intention, in which case one follows the completion of the fruit, and so in every case where the purpose of sowing is not sufficiently clear one follows the completion of the fruit.
he sowed it for greens. For eating the fruit pods while still fresh.
it is tithed for the future. Like vegetables, for which one follows the time of picking.
and he intended it for greens. After sowing he also intended it for greens.

fruits of the second year that were mixed with fruits of the third year. For example, he has a store of second-year fruit and a store of third-year fruit, and found fruit and does not know from where it fell (Chazon Ish, Shevi'it 7:15).
one follows the majority. For it is more reasonable to assume that they fell from the majority (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 8:11).

he separates second tithe from everything etc.. He separates tithe and treats it with the law of second tithe, and need not give it to the poor man. For when there is doubt about the facts as to whether there is an obligation of poor man's tithe here or not, the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow (unlike a doubt in law, such as the avionot above in halachah 7 - Derekh Emunah, based on Chazon Ish, Shevi'it there).
anything exempt from first tithe. As detailed in Hilchot Terumot 2:1-12.

whoever separates terumah or tithe... and whoever, if he separated etc.. Hilchot Terumot 4:1-13 details who is fit to separate terumah ab initio, who is fit after the fact, and who is invalid even after the fact. These laws apply also to second tithe and poor man's tithe.

before they are fixed for tithe... for the first does not fix for the second. Fixing for tithe is the stage at which produce becomes fully obligated in terumot and ma'asrot, and it is forbidden to eat from it even a casual meal before terumot and ma'asrot are separated (see Hilchot Ma'aser 3:1-3). Separating terumah from produce whose processing is complete fixes it for tithes (ibid. 3:3). Here it is explained that separating first tithe does not fix for tithes, so it is permitted to eat casually before separating second tithe (for example where the terumah was separated before the processing was complete, and therefore did not fix for tithes - Jerusalem Talmud Ma'asrot 2:3).

like a firstborn animal. Which also requires being brought to a place, to bring it to the Temple and offer it there, and it is not brought from outside the Land to the Land of Israel (Hilchot Bechorot 1:5).

therefore they did not obligate separating second tithe in Syria. One who bought land in the countries conquered by King David must separate terumot and ma'asrot by rabbinic law (Hilchot Terumot 1:3-4), except for second tithe, which requires being brought to Jerusalem; since it cannot be brought, the Sages did not obligate its separation.

and it appears to me... and likewise it appears to me etc.. In the land of Shinar and the land of Egypt the prophets and Sages enacted separating terumot and ma'asrot (Hilchot Terumot 1:1), and there second tithe must also be separated and its holiness transferred to coins with which food will be bought in Jerusalem (see below 4:1). The Sages enacted this so that the field owners would separate poor man's tithe for the support of the poor of Israel who were found in these countries (unlike Syria - Rikkevo), for if the field owners became accustomed not to separate second tithe, they would also not separate poor man's tithe, which replaces second tithe in the third and sixth years of the Shemittah cycle.
it applies when the Temple exists and when the Temple does not exist. It must be separated both when the Temple is standing and when it is not standing.
from the tradition. The tradition of the Sages.

just as a firstborn animal is eaten only when the Temple exists. For when the Temple exists the firstborn is offered on the altar and afterward eaten by the kohanim (Hilchot Bechorot 1:2; and in our time they wait until it develops a blemish - there 1:10).

the trait of piety... and the Geonim ruled etc.. When the Temple exists there is no need to bring the second-tithe produce itself up to Jerusalem, but one can transfer its holiness to coins equal in value to the produce and buy produce in Jerusalem with those coins (below 4:1). However, after the fact, if he exchanged produce worth a hundred dinars (a "maneh") for the smallest coin (a "perutah"), his act stands (there 4:18). In our time, when the law of eating second-tithe produce does not apply, and so there is no way to use coins that have the holiness of second tithe, it is permitted by strict law to redeem a large amount of produce with a perutah.
this shall not be more severe than consecrated property. For something consecrated to the Temple may be redeemed in our time with a perutah (Hilchot Arachin va'Charamin 8:10).
to the Dead Sea. A sea whose waters are salty and cause the coin to be consumed (the Dead Sea is the Great Sea - ibid. 8:8, according to accurate versions).
he desecrated it. He made the produce non-sacred by transferring its holiness to other produce.
in Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot. Ma'achalot Asurot 10:17.

so too it is not redeemed there and not desecrated. Redemption is the transfer of holiness to money, and desecration is the transfer of holiness to other produce (below 4:1-2). The prohibition against redemption within Jerusalem, and the other laws in this halachah, apply in the time of the Temple (as below halachot 8-9), and because the holiness of Jerusalem is eternal (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:15), these laws apply also in the time of destruction.
for each and every one. Grain, tirosh (wine or grapes), and yitzhar (oil or olives).
he receives three sets of lashes. Three punishments of lashes (each of thirty-nine lashes).

as it says, "you may not etc.". The prohibition of eating outside Jerusalem ("within your gates") applies to second tithe that was brought into Jerusalem, about which it says "and you shall eat before the Lord your God."
rebellious lashes by their decree. Lashes by rabbinic law.
and one who eats outside of this which entered. That is, that he took it out again to the outside.

one does not redeem second tithe etc.. Generally second tithe is redeemed when far from Jerusalem, to save the trouble of carrying the produce. But when it became defiled, it is redeemed even in Jerusalem, because the Sages expounded the verse "for you cannot carry it" also in the sense of eating: when he cannot eat the produce because it became defiled, it is permitted to redeem it even in Jerusalem (Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aser Sheni 3:9, based on Babylonian Talmud Pesachim 36b and others).
inside. Within the wall.
he holds it with a reed. He holds it by means of a long stick.
he is permitted to redeem it there, beside the wall. For it is permitted to redeem anywhere outside the wall, even if not far (see Babylonian Talmud Makkot 19b).
demai. Produce of an am ha'aretz, from which second tithe is separated because of doubt (Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1-2).
for the partitions have already absorbed it. That it entered inside the city wall, and now it must be eaten there and may not be taken out.

as it says, "and you shall eat there before the Lord". This verse deals with food bought with tithe money, and teaches us that it has the law of second-tithe produce that is eaten in Jerusalem. Therefore the Sages forbade taking it out, just as they forbade taking out second-tithe produce.
they must return and be eaten in Jerusalem. For after they have entered Jerusalem there is no way to redeem them (see below 6:16).
and the absorption by the partitions is by their decree. The prohibition of taking out second-tithe produce that entered is not from the Torah but from the words of the Sages.

a tithe whose fifth is not worth a perutah, which is by their decree. One who redeems second tithe must add a fifth to it (below 5:1). However, if the fifth is not worth a perutah he need not add it (below 5:4), and the obligation to eat it in Jerusalem is by rabbinic law.
produce whose processing was completed. The labors done with it in the field were finished and it became obligated in terumot and ma'asrot (see Hilchot Ma'aser chapter 3).

he cannot take out second tithe for them from other produce that did not enter Jerusalem etc.. Since the produce became obligated in terumot and ma'asrot, it is considered as if the second tithe that must be separated from it was already separated ("for gifts that are fit to be separated are as if they were separated" - Hilchot Ma'aser 6:21). Therefore, when the produce passed through Jerusalem, it is as if its second tithe entered Jerusalem and left, and it must be returned and eaten in Jerusalem (Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aser Sheni 3:6). And even if he wishes not to separate the second tithe from the produce that entered, but to separate second tithe for it from other produce, he cannot.

even if he made all this produce second tithe... they all must return and be eaten in Jerusalem. Although generally only a certain percentage of the produce is separated as second tithe, and it is reasonable to say that only this percentage falls under the definition of "fit to be separated," nevertheless the Sages were stringent regarding the law of absorption by the partitions, so that even if he made all the produce second tithe after it left, it has the law of second tithe that entered Jerusalem.
baskets of grapes for the winepress. Grapes intended for making wine that have not yet reached the winepress where they are trodden.
to the drying place. The place where figs are dried.
it is permitted to redeem their second tithe outside. For before the processing is complete they are not in the category of "fit to be separated."

and likewise demai produce etc.. Although it is forbidden to take second tithe out of Jerusalem even if it is of demai (above halachah 9), in this case, where the second tithe has not yet been separated, they were lenient with demai produce.
with an offspring of impurity. Something that became defiled by touching something defined as an "av hatumah" (primary source of impurity) (Hilchot Tumat Met 5:8).

because an offspring of impurity is by their decree. Since the produce is defiled by rabbinic law and pure by Torah law, on one hand they permitted redeeming it even when it is in Jerusalem (like defiled produce above in halachah 8), since it cannot be eaten in purity, and on the other hand they were stringent that it may not be taken out of Jerusalem since it is pure by Torah law. This does not mean that every offspring of impurity defiles food by rabbinic law (for some defile by Torah law - see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:9), but here it speaks of an offspring of impurity whose impurity is rabbinic, for example produce defiled by other food that was defiled (see there 7:1 - Derekh Emunah).
in what case does this apply. That if they became defiled with rabbinic impurity before they entered, it is permitted to eat them outside.
fenugreek. A plant called in our time fenugreek (trigonella).
when sprouting. At the beginning of its growth, when it is still soft and moist.

for thus it is fit for eating. And there is no loss of second tithe in this, although the fenugreek could be improved by cooking and the like (Raavad in his critique, Rikkevo, Aruch HaShulchan 120:15).
vetches of second tithe. Vetches are a type of legume (called in our time bitter vetch) used as animal fodder.

for they are not included among fruits. Vetches are eaten by people only in times of distress (Hilchot Terumot 2:2), and so the Sages were lenient with them regarding the law of absorption by the partitions if he made dough of them, since turning them into dough lowers their importance even further (Kesef Mishneh).

and if they became defiled in Jerusalem they are redeemed and eaten outside. Although second-tithe produce that became defiled with an offspring of impurity inside Jerusalem and was redeemed may not be eaten outside (above halachah 12), with vetch dough they were lenient (Derekh Emunah).
and its foliage. Its branches.
one does not eat second tithe beneath its foliage. Since the wall is what separates the area defined as Jerusalem from the area outside it.

one does not redeem it, for it is like what entered Jerusalem. Regarding redemption the Sages were stringent and treated the area under the foliage as Jerusalem, because the foliage extends from the tree within the wall and follows it.
whose doors are inside the wall and whose interior is outside. The door of the house is within the wall and faces Jerusalem, and part of the house is outside the wall.

one does not eat there and one does not redeem there, to be stringent. One does not eat there since this area is outside the wall, but one also does not redeem there, since the door of the house, which is the main part of the house, is inside the wall. By the same reasoning, where the door of the house is outside the wall, one does not eat even in the inner area since the door is outside, and does not redeem in the inner area because of its location.
and the windows and the thickness of the wall. The space of the windows and the space of the thickness of the wall.

and I have not removed any of it while impure. This sentence is said at the time of the tithe confession (the laws of the confession are explained below in chapter 11), where the one confessing declares that he did not use the tithe while he or it was impure, for example that he did not eliminate it by eating it or by burning it, as below in halachah 2.
rebellious lashes. Lashes by rabbinic law.
and even to light with it etc.. In this law second tithe is more stringent than terumah (see Hilchot Terumot 2:14).
we have already explained. Above 2:8.
and they eat its value etc.. They buy food with it.
as will be explained. Below chapter 7.
when they are tevel. Before terumot and ma'asrot have been separated from them.
in the way that one receives lashes for eating terumah. Hilchot Terumot 7:10.
even though his sun has not set. Although the day has not yet ended, unlike terumah, where a tevul yom may not eat it until nightfall (Hilchot Terumot 7:2).
in aninut by Torah law. During the time that he is an onen by Torah law, as below in halachah 6.
one of the relatives for whom he is obligated to mourn. As detailed in Hilchot Evel 2:1.
and the night. The night following the day of death.
as it says, "and I had eaten etc.". Aaron the kohen wondered how he could eat a sin offering on the day of his sons' death.
and the day of burial does not take hold of its night. When the burial was after the day of death, on the night following the day of burial he is not an onen even by rabbinic law.
all sacred offerings etc.. See also Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 2:7-8.

and it is permitted to eat second tithe of demai in aninut. For the obligation to separate tithe from demai produce is a rabbinic decree, and regarding aninut they did not decree, because it is uncommon (Jerusalem Talmud Demai 1:2).

and to give it to an am ha'aretz. The Sages forbade eating second tithe of demai in impurity because impurity is common (ibid.), but they did not decree against giving it to an am ha'aretz despite the concern that he might eat it in impurity.

provided that he eats its equivalent. He separates from his own money an amount equal to the value of the tithe that he gave to the am ha'aretz, and with this amount buys produce and eats it in Jerusalem as second tithe (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 1:2).
a chaver. A person who is careful in matters of impurity and purity.
he carries any amount of it. He brings even a small quantity up to Jerusalem.
its value. The money with which he redeemed it.
and it is permitted to destroy etc.. That he need not trouble himself to bring it up to Jerusalem.
less than the size of a grogeret. A dried fig.
in crumbs. Crumbled food, which has the quantity of a grogeret only when various pieces are combined.

he gives it to an am ha'aretz and eats its equivalent. He may give it to an am ha'aretz provided that he eats its equivalent (for it is permitted to give him even more than a grogeret, as above in halachah 8), and even though he gave him less than a grogeret, he must eat its equivalent.

but he may not separate it ab initio in order to destroy it. It is forbidden to separate it in a place where he has no way to preserve the second tithe; rather he should wait until he reaches a place where he can preserve it.

for one does not separate in order to destroy. The permission to destroy applies only where a quantity of less than a grogeret happened to come to him, but one may not separate with the intention of destroying.
and anointing is like drinking. Smearing oil on the body has the law of drinking (see also Hilchot Terumot 11:1).
that he buy. That he purchase.
for a met mitzvah. A corpse with no one to bury it.
he eats its equivalent as tithe. He buys produce worth the tithe that he used improperly and eats it in Jerusalem as second tithe.

he eats anything that is normally eaten. This rule includes the laws that follow in the halachah, and also the principle regarding the manner of eating: one eats in the usual manner of eating, for example cooking something normally eaten by cooking (Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aser Sheni 2:1, Aruch HaShulchan 122:5).
except for olives and grapes alone. For wine and oil have special importance, and olives and grapes are grown for the purpose of pressing them.

and one does not perfume the oil. One may not add fragrances and the like that turn it into a medicinal ointment, because this removes it from the category of food (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 11:1, Hilchot Terumot 11:3).
anything that is permitted to non-kohanim to eat in terumah. For example certain peels or certain pits, as detailed in Hilchot Terumot 11:10-13.

lees of second tithe over which water was poured. For example, he had wine of second tithe and the lees remained, and now wants to let the lees sit in water so that the water absorbs the taste of wine.
the first. The first water in which he soaked the lees.

the second is permitted as non-sacred. If he separated the water from the lees and then soaked the lees in other water, this water is non-sacred since the taste of wine in it is weak (unlike terumah, where even the second is forbidden to non-kohanim - Hilchot Terumot 11:13, because terumah is more severe, since it carries a death penalty, and therefore the Sages were stringent with it - Radbaz).
and it improved. That the mixture is worth more than its two parts when separate.

the improvement is by proportion. If he is outside Jerusalem and wants to know for how much money to redeem the wine, he divides the value of the improvement proportionally according to the percentage of wine in the mixture, as below in halachah 15.
kaflotot. A species of leek (Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aser Sheni 2:1).
that he baked it. He baked it with non-sacred wood.
the improvement belongs to the second tithe. To the dough of second tithe.

anything whose improvement is noticeable. That the taste of the non-sacred substance that improved the tithe is noticeable, such as honey and spices, whose taste is noticeable in wine (Or Sameach, and similarly in other commentators).
if it increased in measure. If the weight of the tithe or its volume increased as a result of mixing with the non-sacred substance.
and anything whose improvement is not noticeable. For example dough that he baked, where the taste of the wood is not noticeable in it (ibid.).

they calculate everything as four and a quarter. They calculate the total value of the tithe and the non-sacred before they were mixed, which in our example is four zuzim ("four"), and the value of the improvement added to them, which in our example is one zuz, a quarter of the original value ("a quarter"). And they divide the improvement proportionally: three quarters of it to the tithe and a quarter of it to the non-sacred, so that the tithe must be redeemed for three zuzim and three quarters of a zuz (Merkevet HaMishneh). Some read in the Rambam: "they calculate everything as four zuzim less a quarter" (Rikkevo and Radbaz), and according to this reading the explanation is simple, that one must redeem for four zuzim less a quarter zuz (in any case, the content is agreed by all).
tzinit. A festering wound (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 6:6).
chazazit. A type of boil.
for it was not given for healing. But for pleasurable anointing, which is similar to eating and drinking (Aruch HaShulchan 122:18).
it is not acquired by gift. If he gives it as a gift, it is not acquired by the recipient.
unless he gave him the tevel. If he gives as a gift unseparated produce, it is acquired by the recipient, for before the tithe is separated one cannot say of it that it is property of the Most High.
and one does not betroth a woman with it. Since it is not the property of the man who is betrothing.

and one does not sell it and does not pledge it and does not exchange it. This is the version in most manuscripts, while the printed edition adds: "and one does not give it as collateral," and this detail is also mentioned below in halachah 18 (and see the note of R. Y. Shilat in Mugah Rambam).
and he shall take his second tithe as a pledge. He takes the second tithe from him as a pledge for a debt that he owes him.
they give as collateral. They give a pledge before a loan.
take this tithe and let it be in your hand, and give me non-sacred produce against it. Take the tithe as a pledge and lend me non-sacred produce.

one does not weigh against it even gold dinars. Second tithe whose weight is known may not be placed on one pan of the scale while placing on the other pan something else whose weight one wishes to know, because this is a disgrace to the tithe, which serves as a weight, even if on the other pan he places something valuable such as gold dinars (Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aser Sheni 1:1).

and even to desecrate another second tithe on them, a decree etc.. The Sages decreed even in a case where there is no disgrace to the tithe, for example where the weighing is done for the sake of another tithe, as he wants to know the value of the dinars (by their weight) in order to desecrate it on them.

a decree lest he intend etc.. Lest he use the tithe produce as a permanent weight for other tithes, and over time their weight will diminish (as fruit shrivels), and he will err in calculating the value of the dinars he weighs against them, and desecrate the other tithes for less than their value (Rikkevo, R. Y. Kapach. They were concerned about this specifically with tithe produce because it is not set aside for immediate eating like other produce, and there is a concern that in the meantime it will serve as a weight - Merkevet HaMishneh, Hilchot Chanukah 4:9).
brothers who divided maaser sheni. That they received it as an inheritance.
they may not weigh one against the other. Because of the decree above, halakhah 19.

nor may he give them to a money-changer to show off with them. He may not give them to a money-changer to place on his table to make it look as if he has many coins, since it is forbidden to degrade maaser money by using it for ordinary purposes.

nor may he lend them out to become prominent through them. He may not lend them to a person who wants to appear wealthy. (This is not about an ordinary loan, since it is forbidden to use maaser money that has not been redeemed; rather, the recipient returns the same coins after a time.)

but if he lent them so that they would not rust, it is permitted. It is permitted to lend them if his intent is for their benefit, so that they will not rust, by having the borrower handle them often.
nor may one pay a debt with them etc.. Similarly with maaser ani (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 6:17) and with the money of shemittah produce (Hilchot Shemittah 6:10).

nor may one make a shushvinut with them. A sum of money given to a groom to help with his wedding needs (the details are explained in Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah, chapter 7). It is forbidden to give this sum from maaser sheni money, because if the recipient does not return it to the giver when the giver marries, the giver can sue him in court, so giving a shushvinut is considered a commercial transaction (Tosefta Kifshutah, Peah, p. 189; Daat Aharon).
nor may one repay kindnesses with them. A person who received a favor from his fellow may not give maaser sheni money in return, as that would be like paying a debt.
nor may one pledge charity from them in the synagogue. A person who committed himself to donate a certain sum may not pay his obligation with maaser sheni money.
but one may send from them things that are acts of lovingkindness. In a way that he does his fellow a favor that he is not obligated to do.
and he must inform him. So that the recipient will know that he must treat them with the sanctity of maaser sheni.
but he says to him, Come, let us eat them etc.. In a spirit of love and friendship, and not as payment for effort (Arukh HaShulchan 123:14).
and this is not like payment for his anointing. Since the little oil that was smeared by the friend has no significant monetary value (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 2:2).
as we have already explained. Above, halakhah 17.

that one who steals maaser sheni does not pay double, and one who robs it does not pay the added fifth. One who steals from his fellow, and witnesses testify to it, must return the value of what he stole plus an equal amount again. One who robs his fellow and swears falsely that he did not rob, and afterwards admits it, must pay the value of the robbery plus a fifth. These additions do not apply to maaser sheni, which is property of the Most High, just as they do not apply to one who steals or robs consecrated property. (For theft, see Hilchot Genevah 2:1; for robbery, see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 5:1, that one does not swear regarding consecrated property, and Hilchot Gezelah 8:14, that no fifth is paid for something regarding which one does not swear.)
for the maintenance of the Temple. For the property of the Temple.

whoever redeems it may redeem it etc.. A person who wishes to redeem it must pay its value to the Temple maintenance fund, and after the redemption the sanctity of maaser sheni still remains on it, and he must eat it in Jerusalem or redeem it.
at their value. At their worth.

and if he did not specify, but merely set aside money corresponding to the produce, it is sufficient. Because the circumstances show that his intention is to redeem (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 4:7).
and spend it there. He should buy food with it, as detailed below, chapter 7.

who deconsecrated money onto produce. Money with which he redeemed maaser sheni, and afterwards he deconsecrated it onto other produce. Ideally, however, one should not deconsecrate money onto produce (below, halakhah 6).
does not require a blessing. Just as one does not recite a blessing when separating demai (Hilchot Maaser 9:4).

one does not redeem it in the name of maaser etc.. When redeeming maaser with money, one must first assess the value of the produce. It should not be assessed by the price a person in the market would give for it as maaser produce, since by such an assessment its value is very low, because the buyer has to bring it up to Jerusalem; rather it should be assessed by the price one could get for similar ordinary produce (Arukh HaShulchan 124:16-17).
so that it will not be degraded. So that the monetary value of the produce will not decrease (ibid.).

one may not deconsecrate maaser sheni money onto other money. Since the permission to transfer the sanctity of the maaser to money is because of the burden of carrying it to Jerusalem, as stated explicitly in the Torah (see above, halakhah 1), the Sages forbade a deconsecration that does not ease the burden, such as money onto money, and all the more so money onto produce, as below, halakhah 6 (Arukh HaShulchan 126:4; and see also below, 5:13).
and if he deconsecrated, the produce is brought up and eaten in Jerusalem. And it cannot be redeemed (see also below, 7:1-2).
the maaser has not been acquired. The sanctity does not take effect on the animals, and the money retains its sanctity.
lest he raise herds from them. That the animals will multiply and he will not guard them with the sanctity of maaser.
in a time of pressing need. In a case of special need, such as that he needs to use the silver money for his needs.

not that he should keep it etc.. Because copper coins are inferior coins and this is not honorable for the maaser; also copper coins rust quickly, and the maaser might suffer loss (Rashi, Bava Metzia 56a).
until he finds relief. Until other silver coins come into his hands (Rik"u).
with silver. With coins.
if he redeemed for himself and added a fifth. As below, 5:1.
only with stamped silver that has an image or inscription. For the word "vetzarta" is also expounded from the word "tzurah" (form) (Bavli, Bava Metzia 47b).
with a tongue of silver. A piece of silver.
and one does not redeem with less than a perutah. With coins each of which is worth less than a perutah, even though their total is large (Rik"u, Kesef Mishneh).
that is not current. That is not in circulation.
and in that place. In the place where the redeemer is located; it does not help if the coin is current in another country (see below, halakhah 14).
the earlier kings. A previous regime.

if it is current in their name. If the people of the country still trade with it on the basis of its stamp (and not according to other qualities such as its weight), and the present regime does not prohibit the use of the coin.

with money that is not in his possession. Meaning he has no reasonable way to reach it, for example because it is in a dangerous place or he lent it out. But if it is in his house, or even deposited with another person, it is considered in his possession (Arukh HaShulchan 125:5; Daat Aharon).
in your hand. That is in your possession.
and a robber. A bandit.
with great difficulty. With great effort.
he has said nothing. Because in his heart he has given up on the money and it is no longer his.

he must be concerned about everything he redeemed with it retroactively. Perhaps the money was lost before he redeemed, so if the produce still exists, he must redeem it again out of doubt (see Hilchot Terumot 5:26, Hilchot Maaser 7:4).
he may not deconsecrate onto them. Because they are not coins in circulation in the place where the one deconsecrating is located.

if he had coins of the Tiberias mint in Babylonia, he may deconsecrate onto them. Even though the money is in Babylonia and he is in Tiberias, he may deconsecrate onto it because it is current in the place where the one deconsecrating is located. [Note: the Rambam in his Commentary on the Mishnah vocalizes this word Teverayah.]

maaser sheni is deconsecrated onto a sela that will come up in my hand from this purse. His intention is that the redemption take effect after the sela comes into his hand (Rabbi Y. Kafih; Daat Aharon).

onto a sela that I will break from this gold dinar. Onto one sela of the selas I will receive from the money-changer in exchange for the dinar; his intention is that the redemption take effect at the time he has one sela in his hand (ibid.).
pundyon. A small coin whose value relative to a sela is 1/48.
onto the sela that was in my son's hand. And he does not know whether the sela is still in his son's possession.
he has not deconsecrated etc.. It is forbidden to eat the produce until he checks whether the sela was in his son's possession at the time of the deconsecration (Arukh HaShulchan 125:20).
he has said nothing. And the redemption has not taken effect.
nor has he designated the maaser. His statement is not considered a separation of maaser.
but if he designated and said etc.. That is, he specified a certain place for the maaser within the produce, even though he did not actually separate it (see also Hilchot Terumot 3:8).
and he may redeem at the cheap price. He is permitted to redeem the maaser according to the low rate.

as the shopkeeper buys. According to the wholesale price that a shopkeeper pays for goods he orders for his store. The reason for the permission is that the Torah promised blessing regarding maaser sheni (see Deuteronomy 14:24), and from this they learned that the redemption is done in a way that brings blessing to its owner (Yerushalmi, Maaser Sheni 4:3).

and he gives the coins as the money-changer breaks them down. When a person has small coins of maaser sheni which he wants to deconsecrate onto a sela coin, he may deconsecrate a large number of small coins according to the amount a money-changer gives a customer when the money-changer hands over a large coin and receives small coins (this act is called "poret" in the Rambam's language; see Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 4:2; Arukh HaShulchan 125:22).

not as he combines them. When the money-changer gives small coins and receives a large coin in return ("matzaref"), he gives a relatively small number of small coins. In deconsecrating small coins of maaser, the one deconsecrating need not calculate according to this amount.
and if he transgressed and redeemed etc.. See above 2:2, that nowadays it is permitted to redeem this way ab initio.
a sixth. A sixth of its weight.
passes with difficulty. That one can find sellers who will accept it as payment for their goods.

he may deconsecrate onto it ab initio etc.. In the laws of purchase and sale, a deviation of one sixth from the true price does not void the sale (see Hilchot Mechirah 12:2-4). Maaser sheni may be redeemed at the cheap rate (as above, halakhah 18), so one need not be strict about a deficiency that is not grounds for voiding a sale (Daat Aharon).
and it was found to be bad. That it is lacking more than a sixth.
he should exchange it. He should deconsecrate onto another coin.
approximately. By an inexact estimate.
it is redeemed by the word of one. One person who will assess its value (meaning a person who is expert in the field and knows how to assess; Arukh HaShulchan 125:24; Daat Aharon).
merchants. Traders.
even if one of them was a gentile etc.. For this is neither testimony nor a legal judgment, which would be invalid for gentiles or relatives, but only a clarification of the facts.

and the owners are compelled to open first. To offer a price for maaser whose value is not known, and to redeem it himself if no one is found willing to redeem at a higher price; for if the owner redeems it himself, he adds a fifth, as below, 5:1 (Daat Aharon).

and this is a stricter rule for maaser than for hekdesh. For one who consecrates an animal for the altar and it develops a blemish, he is not compelled to redeem it (Arukh HaShulchan 125:26; and see Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 5:1-3, that with Temple-maintenance consecrations the owners are compelled to redeem, except for an inherited field when the jubilee is in force; and see Tosefta Kifshutah, Maaser Sheni, p. 753, who proposed a different explanation).

one does not carry maaser produce from place to place to redeem it there. Some wrote that the reason is the degradation of maaser sheni (Arukh HaShulchan 125:28, and see Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 3:19).
and one who carries it etc.. If he transgressed and carried it (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 4:1).
redeems at the price of the place of redemption. According to the price in the place of the redemption.

he redeems it at the cheap price, since they were fit to be sold cheaply. Even though at the time of redemption they are in a place where prices are high, he redeems them according to the cheap place since it was possible to redeem them there, for with demai they were lenient.
at the threshing floor. At the place where the crop is gathered.
expenses from his house. Expenses from his own money.
and improved it. That the value of the produce in the city is higher.
and lost his expenses. That he cannot deduct them from the redemption sum, since he could have redeemed at the threshing floor and caused himself a loss (compare below, 9:6).

whether it was given to him as untithed produce as a gift, as we explained. Above, 3:17: one who receives maaser sheni as a gift does not acquire it unless he received untithed produce and tithed it himself.
if it was worth four, he gives five. For the fifth is a fifth of the total after the addition ("a fifth from the outside"), and relative to the principal it is a quarter.
and if a man redeems any of his tithe. And the verse continues: "he shall add a fifth to it."
and a woman who redeemed her maaser. Maaser from produce that she owns.
from tradition. The Sages' tradition in the interpretation of Scripture.
redeemed the redemption of maaser produce. He redeemed maaser money, transferring its sanctity to other money (though ideally one should not do this, as above, 4:5).
adds a fifth. To the principal, but not to the fifth, as explained immediately below.

adds a second fifth to the principal only and does not add a fifth on the fifth. For example, if the produce was worth four and he redeemed it for five, in the second redemption he adds one more, and not one and a quarter.
maaser sheni whose fifth is not worth a perutah. And the obligation to eat it in Jerusalem is rabbinic (above, 2:9).
whose value is not known. And there is no way to determine its price from three merchants (see above, 4:20).
any maaser that is not itself, and its redemption money, his own does not add a fifth. The obligation of a fifth applies only where the produce is his and the redemption money is his.

if its fifth is not worth a perutah, it is enough that he says etc.. He need not set aside an additional coin for the maaser whose fifth is not worth a perutah, but may redeem it onto money with which he already redeemed. This is because a person usually cannot tighten his money to exact amounts: he redeems onto money worth slightly more (so as not to stumble in eating unredeemed maaser), and for that slight excess he may redeem the maaser whose fifth is not worth a perutah.

it and its fifth are deconsecrated. Although by strict law he is not obligated in a fifth, as above, halakhah 4, when he redeems onto other maaser money he also mentions the fifth in order to beautify the mitzvah (Arukh HaShulchan 127:11).
and one who redeems maaser for more than its value. One who exchanges maaser produce for money worth more than the value of the produce.
the excess does not take on the sanctity of maaser. Rather part of the money remained ordinary (and see Rik"u, that this sentence is a continuation and explanation of the previous halakhah).
the householder says for a sela. The owner of the produce offers to redeem it for a sela.

because he added to the principal. Although a sela and a perutah is less than a sela and a fifth, he takes precedence over the owner, because the fifth can be avoided, as below, halakhah 8 (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 4:3).

it is permitted to employ a stratagem regarding the redemption of one's maaser. To use a permitted method to avoid the obligation of giving the fifth. The reason for the permission is that the Torah promised blessing regarding maaser sheni (see Deuteronomy 14:24), and from this they learned that the redemption is done in a way that brings blessing to its owner (Yerushalmi, Maaser Sheni 4:3).
adults. Who have reached the age of majority (Hilchot Ishut 2:1, 2:10) and have independent ability in monetary acquisition.
and for his Hebrew slave. A Jewish slave is treated like a hired worker, in that only the product of his labor belongs to the master (not his person), and he has independent monetary acquisition.
here, take these coins. Take them and acquire them.
and redeem the maaser for yourself with them. Redeem my produce with them for your own benefit.

but he may not say to him, redeem for me with them. Because this wording implies that he is not giving him ownership of the money but making him an agent for the redemption, and an agent adds a fifth.
because their hand is like his hand. For anything they acquire belongs to their father or master.
for a Hebrew maidservant is a minor. For when she becomes a na'arah she goes free (Hilchot Avadim 4:5).

and a minor cannot acquire for others except in something that is rabbinic. He cannot acquire on behalf of others something that is Torah-law (see also Hilchot Eruvin 1:20, Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 4:7). And redeeming another person's maaser sheni is treated as acquiring for others (Chiddushei Rabbi Chaim HaLevi, Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 4:6).

while it is still untithed. And the recipient separates the tithes, and afterwards the giver deconsecrates the maaser sheni onto his own money, and does not need to add a fifth since the produce is not his.
a woman who brought in to her husband. At the time of marriage, or that she inherited from her family.
as we explained. Above, 3:17.
even on Shabbat. For eating on it is a mitzvah (Rashi, Bava Metzia 54a).
to combine them into gold dinars. To exchange many coins for a few coins of equal value.
combines. Ab initio, unlike what was stated above, 4:5, that one does not deconsecrate money onto money, because here he deconsecrates in order to carry it to Jerusalem (Arukh HaShulchan 126:4-5).
and if he combined them for himself, he does not add a fifth. Unlike what was stated above, 5:3, regarding one who redeems maaser money for himself.
for this is not the way of redemption. For in an ordinary redemption one removes the thing from its sanctity in order to use it as ordinary, but here his intention is only to ease their burden.

one who breaks a sela etc.. A person who needs to break a large coin into copper small coins should not break all of it at once, but first break half in silver (a shekel is half a sela) and half in copper (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 2:8-9). The reason for the law is the honor of the maaser and its loss (see above, 4:7); here they permitted breaking half because he does so to buy food in Jerusalem or, in a time of pressing need, outside Jerusalem.

it is permitted to deconsecrate maaser silver etc.. Above, 4:5, it was said that one does not deconsecrate maaser silver onto other silver. Here the case is that he has a little maaser produce that he wishes to deconsecrate onto a significant coin; then it is permitted ab initio to add maaser silver to complete the sum (Rik"u, Radbaz, and Chazon Ish, Demai 3:4, and in accord with the Raavad's critique).
he does not deconsecrate everything onto one sela. Since he can deconsecrate the produce onto a silver dinar, which is also a relatively significant coin.
and gathered from here and there. He gathered them one by one at random.

whatever he gathered, he gathered for the maaser until he completes. For each coin he gathers there is doubt whether it is maaser, so they were strict to treat it as maaser until he has gathered a number of coins equal to the number of maaser coins he had.

and if he mixed and took a handful. If he mixed the coins (before or after they fell, per Radbaz) and gathered several coins together in his hand, so that certainly ordinary coins came up in his hand as well.

or gathered from one side. He gathered only from one place, so he certainly gathered ordinary coins too, for it is impossible that all the maaser fell on only one side (Arukh HaShulchan 128:6; Daat Aharon).
and found it lacking, it is proportionate. Even though he did not find all the coins, they did not rule strictly to give the maaser all that he had; rather they divide proportionally.
and he stipulates and says etc.. This stipulation is needed in all the cases brought in this halakhah.
and the ordinary one. And the ordinary sela.
he brings coins worth a sela. He brings coins whose value is a sela.
the better of the two. The better sela.

and he deconsecrates the copper coins onto it. For the sanctity of the maaser should not be left in copper coins, as above, 4:7 (and the reason he must bring copper coins and cannot simply take the better sela from the mixture ab initio and say that if it is ordinary then the other sela is deconsecrated onto it, is that deconsecrating a coin onto an identical coin is not a way of deconsecration and should not be done even in a time of pressing need, Rik"u).
these are ordinary. And we do not worry that what he found is the maaser that was moved from its place.
a maneh. One hundred dinars.

the rest is ordinary. We assume that the maneh of maaser remained in its place, and the father added to it another maneh of ordinary money, and that when he said "there is a maneh there" he referred only to the maaser money (Rik"u). So there are a hundred of maaser and a hundred of ordinary mixed together, and they are to be deconsecrated in the manner explained above, halakhah 2 (Daat Aharon, based on the Rishonim).

there are two hundred there, and he found a maneh, it is ordinary. The dinars he found are ordinary, since people do not usually separate maaser coins from each other, as they must bring them all up to Jerusalem (Rashi, Beitzah 10b); so it is reasonable to assume that he did not take a hundred dinars out of the two hundred, but took all the maaser silver together, and the dinars he found are other dinars.

if he left a maneh of maaser and found two hundred... all is ordinary. If the father himself found two hundred, we should not assume that he added a maneh of ordinary money to the maaser, for if he had done so he would have remembered it (see Rashi there, that placing ordinary coins with maaser coins is an unusual act); rather we assume these are other coins (Rik"u).
purses. Something like wallets.
and was found in another corner. Produce or coins.
he may not eat from the small ones. He may not use the money in the small purses.
who became speechless. Who became mute.
and nodded his head. As a sign of agreement.
they examine him three times, as they examine for divorce documents. They ask him three questions to test whether his mind is clear enough (see Hilchot Gerushin 2:16).

the maaser sheni of your father that you are seeking etc.. That he had been searching for money his father left him and did not know where it was, and it was told to him in a dream where it was and how much, and that this money was maaser sheni (Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 10:7).

words of dreams neither raise nor lower. They have no halakhic force either to be lenient or to be strict. Even though part of what was told to him in the dream turned out true, this does not prove that all its details are correct (see Rik"u), so the money he found has the law of ordinary money, which is ordinary.
even if you die. Of hunger.
these are ordinary. And we do not worry that he told them not to touch the money because it is maaser.

if as those who are deceiving etc.. One must distinguish between a case where the circumstances show that the father said this as one giving testimony or a will and meant what he said, and a case where it appears that he said it so that they would not waste the money or for some other incidental reason.

and if it was of metal, it and what is in it is an offering. We assume the vessel was donated to the Temple's property, and what is in it is also sacred, since people do not usually put ordinary things in a sacred vessel (Mishnah Maaser Sheni 4:10). A clay vessel, however, is usually not consecrated since it has no importance, so only its contents are sacred (Peirush HaMishnayot there).
in a time of danger. When the gentiles decreed against the observance of mitzvot, and out of habit this practice continued even after the danger (Responsa Maharik, no. 161).

even gold dinars with silver or with coins. Although people are not accustomed to placing ordinary gold coins together with silver or with copper coins, we should not worry that this silver is maaser (Yerushalmi, Maaser Sheni 4:6; and see the commentators on Mishnah Maaser Sheni 4:9).

since the markets of Jerusalem are swept every day. They are cleaned every day, so even if the money is found immediately after the festival, it does not have the law of money found at the time of the festival, which is maaser.
but at the time of the festival, everything is maaser. For all Israel goes up for the festival then, and everyone who has maaser sheni money brings it up (Peirush HaMishnayot, Shekalim 7:2).
always maaser. All the days of the year.
most of the people. Most of the buyers who are animal dealers.

for their presumption is from the terumah of the chamber, which the treasurers deconsecrated onto the animal. Most of the money found on the Temple Mount comes from the money donated as half-shekels and placed in the chamber designated for it ("terumat halishkah," see Hilchot Shekalim 2:4), and it is ordinary because the treasurers take money out of the terumah of the chamber only by deconsecrating it onto an animal for an offering (ibid. 3:15).
if most of those who deposit maaser. If most of the people who placed money in it placed maaser money.
half and half. They were found exactly in the middle.
are eaten according to the stringencies of both. For a doubt in Torah law is resolved stringently.
and require washing of the hands. Washing the hands (Hilchot Terumot 11:7).
and sunset. Explained above, 3:4.
to an onen. Explained above, 3:6.
bringing to the place. To Jerusalem.

are eaten according to their stringency. That one may not apply to them the lenient laws that apply to the maaser sheni of demai (such as eating in a state of aninut or giving to an am ha'aretz, as above, 3:8).
he eats everything in purity in the place. If it was found in Jerusalem.

therefore if they became mixed in Jerusalem etc.. Since in Jerusalem there is a way to permit them by eating them in purity, they considered the maaser there as something that has those who permit it. And although an impure person and an animal cannot eat it, and for them there is no way of permission, since a pure person can eat it there easily it is considered something that has permitters (Peirush HaMishnayot, Bikkurim 2:2; Daat Aharon; and see also Hilchot Bikkurim 4:15). All this applies to a mixture of a kind with its own kind ("b'mino"). But in a mixture of a kind with a different kind, the ruling is according to imparting flavor, even for something that has permitters (Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:12).

one who sows maaser sheni after it has entered Jerusalem, the growth is maaser sheni. Since there is an easy way to eat it in Jerusalem in purity, the Sages ruled strictly that it is not permitted by sowing (Peirush HaMishnayot, Bikkurim 2:2).

but if he sowed it before it entered, the growth is ordinary. Since it grows both from the power of the maaser sheni and from the power of the ground which is ordinary, and "a thing with two causes, one forbidden and one permitted, what results from both is permitted" (below, 10:21).
even in something whose seed does not disintegrate. That when it is sown it does not rot in the ground.

and one redeems it at the time of its sowing. Ab initio, a person who wishes to sow maaser sheni must redeem it before sowing (though if he transgressed and sowed without redemption, the crops are ordinary as explained in this halakhah; and see also Hilchot Me'ilah 5:11).

and the partitions fell. So that it can no longer be eaten within the walls of Jerusalem, for example if the Temple was destroyed after he had taken the maaser out, since maaser sheni is eaten only before the Temple, as above, 2:1 (though if the Temple stands and the walls fell, maaser sheni is eaten; see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:15).
even though it is not worth a perutah. That is rabbinic, yet it still has the law of absorbing the partitions and it is forbidden to redeem it after it has entered (as above, 2:9).
as we explained in Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot. Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot, chapter 15.
that which is purchased. That was acquired.
are not redeemed at a distance. It is forbidden to redeem them even when they are far from Jerusalem and have not yet entered it.
with a primary source of impurity. With Torah-level impurity (see above, 2:12 and the commentary there).

this is a stricter rule for what was bought with maaser money than for maaser produce itself. For maaser produce is redeemed outside Jerusalem, while produce bought with maaser money is stricter in this matter. As for the reason, the Arukh HaShulchan (130:4) writes that he committed a transgression by buying produce with maaser money outside Jerusalem, for ab initio one does not deconsecrate maaser money onto produce (see above, 4:6).

and if they became impure through a derivative of impurity, they are redeemed and eaten in Jerusalem. If they became impure with rabbinic impurity, they required that they be redeemed so that maaser not be eaten in impurity, and required that they be eaten in Jerusalem because they were bought with maaser money and by Torah law they are still pure (see also above, 2:12 and the commentary there).
whose growth is from the earth. This includes cattle and sheep that grow from eating the plants of the earth (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 1:5).
the growth of whose growth is from the earth. As below, halakhah 5.
truffles. A kind of mushroom.
because their growth is not from the earth. For they have no roots by which they draw from the earth.
produce that cannot reach Jerusalem. That might rot.
they are the growth of its growth. They come from animals that grow from plants.
temed. Water that has been left standing on grape pomace.
before it turned sour. Before its fermentation was complete (Rashi, Eruvin 27b).

if he bought it before it turned sour and it turned sour, he has acquired maaser. Even though its fermentation was completed only after his purchase, the law of maaser sheni applies to it and the money becomes ordinary, since at the time of purchase it already had the potential to ferment (Bavli, Chullin 26a and Rashi there).

when he put in three of water and found less than four. For example, he put three logs of water on the grape pomace, and after some time found less than four logs, which is a sign that a very thin wine was formed, which is not considered wine until it turns sour.
if he put in three and drew out four, it is like diluted wine. See also Hilchot Maaser 2:7.
tender tips of thistles and carobs. The tops of soft branches and the tips of carobs at the time the trees blossom.
before they have sweetened. Before they are prepared for eating by pickling (Peirush HaMishnayot, Shevi'it 7:5; Uktzin 3:4).
luf. A kind of onion.
whether after they have sweetened or before they have sweetened, they may be bought. Since they are fit for eating even before pickling.
and the kor. The soft part at the top of the palm tree, which is fit for human consumption.
saffron. A plant from which a yellow spice is produced.
heads of spices. All the aromatic plants (Peirush HaMishnayot, Uktzin 3:5).
and peppers. Black pepper.
and costus. A plant from which perfume is produced.
and asafoetida. A seasoning plant in cold countries (ibid.).
and the leaves of hari'a. Hari'a is safflower, and the leaves of hari'a are a certain part of the plant used for coloring dishes (ibid.).
dill. A vegetable (today called shamir) used to give flavor to a dish and afterwards removed from it.
for kamakh. For crushing and placing in a food called kutach.
muries. A salty seasoning sometimes made from fish.
and he absorbs the price of the water and the salt into the price of the oil. He pays the seller a high price for the oil in order to cover the price of the water and salt as well.

because he reduces its eating and the eating of it etc.. He narrows the possibilities of eating the maaser ("its eating") and of eating the terumah ("the eating of it"), since each has restrictions that the other does not, as he goes on to detail.

for only kohanim eat it, those who have waited for sunset etc.. Terumah is eaten only by kohanim who have immersed and only after the day has darkened and their purification is complete; on the other hand, it is permitted to an onen (on the day of death of one of his relatives), and there is no restriction on the place of eating it. With maaser the laws are the reverse (see above, 3:4-6).

because peace offerings are eaten by non-kohanim. Although parts of the animal are offered on the altar or given to the kohanim, they were not concerned about that, since the main part of the meat is given to the owner of the offering. Nor were they concerned that the meat of peace offerings is eaten only for two days and one night, since one does not usually keep meat longer than that lest it spoil (Arukh HaShulchan 131:2).
in order to keep it away from the altar. So that they would not lose the parts of the animal that are not given to the owner of the offering.
the court decreed etc.. Since the main mitzvah of maaser sheni money is to buy a peace offering with it (Rosh, Maaser Sheni 1:3; and see Sifrei Devarim, section 107; Yerushalmi, Maaser Sheni 1:2).
which are not fit for peace offerings. Therefore they did not decree about them, just as they did not decree about buying produce.
because he is obligated to clear out. To destroy the produce at the time that that species is finished in the field.
as will be explained. Hilchot Shemittah 7:1.
one who buys water and salt etc.. A person who bought food items that may not be bought with maaser money (as above, halakhah 4).

the maaser has not been acquired, even though the money became ordinary. Although the act of acquisition took place and the money becomes ordinary, sanctity does not take effect on the thing he bought (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 1:5). So he has freed himself of the obligation to eat in the sanctity of maaser, but has lost the fulfillment of the mitzvah (Arukh HaShulchan 131:9).
one who buys produce outside Jerusalem with maaser money. Contrary to the law (see above, 4:6).

if inadvertently, the seller is compelled to return the money to the owners. For we assume that had the buyer known that the money in his hand was maaser money, he would not have bought produce with it outside Jerusalem, since this causes him the trouble of bringing the produce up to Jerusalem; therefore this purchase is considered a mistaken purchase.
the produce is brought up and eaten in Jerusalem. For the sanctity has passed to the produce, and it cannot be redeemed unless it became impure, as above, halakhah 1.

if inadvertently the money returns to its place; if deliberately it is brought up and eaten in Jerusalem. So the text in the printed editions, in accord with what was said in the previous halakhah. In manuscripts the reading is reversed: "deliberately the money returns to its place; inadvertently it is brought up and eaten in Jerusalem," and the Rik"u and Kesef Mishneh already noted that this reading is mistaken (and see the note of Rabbi Y. Shilat in Rambam Meduyak).
the money returns to its place. The seller is compelled to return it, and it has its sanctity, as above, halakhah 15.
it is buried, it and its hide. After its death it must be buried together with its hide so that no one will benefit from it (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 1:6).

if he bought slaves and land etc.. When he bought things not fit for eating, the sanctity of maaser sheni does not pass to them, and even if he did so deliberately the money remains with its sanctity (similarly with shemittah money; see Hilchot Shemittah 6:10).
if the seller fled. And it is impossible to get the money back and return the purchase.

he eats the equivalent of that money in Jerusalem as maaser. He buys food worth the money he used not for eating and eats it in Jerusalem with the law of maaser sheni (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 1:7).
for meat of desire. To eat it without offering it as a peace offering, which the Sages forbade, as above, halakhah 12.
like one who bought an ox for plowing. The acquisition does not take effect, as explained in the previous halakhah.
and they did not acquire peace offerings. The animal or beast was not consecrated as a peace offering (for the beast is not fit for this, and the animal was not bought for this purpose).
the sanctity of maaser left it. Like food that spoiled (above, 3:11), since there is no way to offer it and eat it with the sanctity of maaser.
and he redeems it. From the sanctity of a peace offering, like an offering that developed a blemish (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:6).

and nevertheless if he redeemed it for himself he adds a fifth. Although the sanctity of maaser left it and he need not add a fifth under the law of redeeming maaser, he must still add a fifth under the law of redeeming sacred items (as explained in Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 7:4; Kesef Mishneh. And see Radbaz and Arukh HaShulchan 131:12, who explained the novelty in this case in additional ways).
one who designates maaser money for peace offerings. He earmarked his money for buying peace offerings.
they have not become peace offerings. And he may buy whatever foods he wishes with the money.

for the sanctity of a peace offering does not take effect on the sanctity of maaser etc.. The sanctity of a peace offering takes effect only when he buys with maaser sheni silver an animal to offer as a peace offering and eat, which the Torah considered a purchase for eating. But he cannot consecrate the maaser money itself or maaser produce (so that they would buy peace offerings with the money received for the produce), since they are property of the Most High and not his.
as ordinary food. For example, outside Jerusalem.
he will cry out to Heaven. He should seek atonement for his sin, since there is no practical way to correct it.
the money returns to its place etc.. One acts as explained above, halakhah 17.
from one who is not a merchant and is not particular. From a person who is not a trader, and who sets the price only according to the meat.

the hide became ordinary. The sanctity of maaser sheni did not take effect on it, and it need not be redeemed, since the maaser money was given for the meat, and incidentally the seller also gave the hide.
the hide did not become ordinary. And he must deconsecrate it and eat foods of its value with the sanctity of maaser sheni.

and likewise one who buys sealed jars of wine in a place where they are customarily sold sealed. In a place where it is customary to sell the wine together with the container and one does not pay for the container itself.
from one who is not a merchant. That the seller is not a merchant who is particular about the value of the jar.

therefore the seller must open the mouths of the jars so that the vessel will not become ordinary. Even when the seller is not a merchant and sold sealed jars, there is still room to worry that he also took the price of the vessel into account, in which case the vessel does not become ordinary; therefore it is proper for the seller to open the jar so that it will be clear that the vessel did not become ordinary (Daat Aharon, in explanation of the halakhah).

and if he wished to be strict with himself and sell by measure, the vessel became ordinary. If the seller wished to be strict with himself and set the price only by the measure of wine, he need not open the jars, for then it is clear that the vessel became ordinary (ibid.).
he bought them open. In which case it is not customary to sell the jar along with the wine.
or sealed in a place where they are customarily sold open. Where it is not customary to sell the container along with the wine, so he paid for the container separately with maaser sheni money.

the money for the vessel did not become ordinary. For the vessel is not secondary to the produce, since the way is to buy produce without a container (Rik"u and Radbaz); so part of the money the seller received is still sacred, and the buyer must deconsecrate it.
their peels became ordinary. For peels have no independent importance, and the same is true of a date basket and of crushed baskets of dates, where the packaging is nullified to its contents.
date basket. A woven basket made of twigs and the like, used to pack moist fruit when selling it.
baskets. Large baskets.
crushed. Squashed.
and if they are not crushed, the baskets did not become ordinary. For dates that are not crushed do not need a basket, and the basket has the law of the fig baskets above, halakhah 3.
and he lent his jars to that maaser. That he put the wine in them temporarily, and said explicitly that this was his intention (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 3:12).
the maaser did not acquire the jars. The sanctity of maaser did not take effect on them.
he gathered the wine into them without specification. That he did not say he was placing it temporarily.
if he named it etc.. If he placed untithed wine in the jars, made it maaser sheni, and afterwards sealed the jars.
and if after he sealed their mouths etc.. If he made the wine maaser sheni after he sealed the jars, it appears from his actions that he intends to nullify the jars to the maaser.
he deposited in the jar a revi'it of ordinary. That he did not make all of it maaser sheni, but left a quarter-log of ordinary wine.
brine. The liquid from pickled fish that he bought with maaser sheni money.
even after he sealed. Even if he made them maaser sheni after he sealed.
the maaser did not acquire the jars. For other liquids besides wine are not of great importance, and in all cases the jar is not nullified to them (also in the cases brought above, halakhot 2-3).

it is buried in its hide. For all of it is forbidden for benefit, and it cannot be redeemed since its flesh is fit only for dogs to eat, and sacred items are not redeemed to feed dogs (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 3:11; Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:10).
it is redeemed etc.. For from the moment it was slaughtered it has the law of food.
like other maaser produce that became impure. As above, 2:8, 7:1.

to eat against it until it becomes ordinary. To deconsecrate it onto foods and eat them in Jerusalem with the sanctity of maaser, until he has deconsecrated the value of the dinar and it has become ordinary.

he must eat against it for twenty ma'ah etc.. The value of half a dinar now, for before the money became cheaper he had eaten the value of half a dinar and must complete the other half. The same applies in a case where money became more expensive: he completes half a dinar according to its value now.

one who buys produce etc.. The principle in this halakhah and the following ones is that, regarding purchase and sale, the acquisition takes effect at the time of pulling the produce, whereas the deconsecration of maaser money takes effect at the time of giving the money.
and did not manage to give the sela until the produce became more expensive and stood at two. Before he paid, the price of the produce rose to two selas.

he separates for them only a sela etc.. After paying the seller the sela that he owes him (the value of the produce at the time of pulling), he separates a sela from his maaser sheni money and deconsecrates it too onto this produce, since the time of deconsecration is the time of giving the money ("by giving the money he acquires"), and at this time the produce is worth two selas; so the owner of the maaser gained from the rise in price ("and the profit goes to the maaser"), as he takes an additional sela out to ordinary status (so it emerges from Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 4:6, and so explained Arukh HaShulchan 133:11 and Chazon Ish, Shevi'it 10:13).

and he shall give the money and it shall stand for him. The wording of the verse is: "He shall add a fifth of the money of your valuation to it, and it shall be his" (Leviticus 27:19), and the quotation here follows the language of the Sages in several places (such as Tosefta Arachin 4:4, Bavli Shabbat 128a, and see Tosafot there, s.v. venatan hakesef).
he pulled produce worth two selas. Produce whose price is two selas.
he separates for them from maaser sheni money only a sela. The price of the produce at the time of giving the money, which is the time of deconsecration.
and adds to it a second sela from ordinary and gives it to the seller. Since in terms of the laws of purchase and sale he owes him two selas, the price of the produce at the time of pulling.
what he redeemed he redeemed. The sela became ordinary at the time it was given, and the produce was seized by the sanctity of maaser.

and the law is between them. In terms of the laws of purchase and sale, the seller may forgo his loss, or cancel the sale and receive the curse of "mi shepara" in court for not standing by his word (see Hilchot Mechirah 7:1-2).

for the redemption of maaser sheni is its pulling. In terms of the laws of maaser, the giving of the money ("its redemption," Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 4:6) is the determining act, just as pulling is the determining act in the laws of purchase and sale.

if he had maaser money in Jerusalem etc.. The permission to deconsecrate maaser money onto ordinary produce applies only in Jerusalem, meaning when at least one of the two is in Jerusalem, either the money, as in this halakhah, or the produce, as in the previous halakhah; but when both the money and the produce are outside Jerusalem, one does not deconsecrate ab initio, as above, 4:6.
to what does this apply etc.. As explained above, 3:8.

and it is permitted to deconsecrate maaser sheni onto the produce of an am ha'aretz and onto his money. A chaver who obtained produce or money of an am ha'aretz may deconsecrate maaser sheni onto them, since they have the presumption of being ordinary.
one who sets aside a dinar of maaser to eat against it as he goes. As above, halakhah 6.
less than a perutah became ordinary. For this amount has no importance in any matter of the Torah (Peirush HaMishnayot, Maaser Sheni 4:8).
of demai. To which a fifth is not added (as above, 5:4).

such as when less than four fifths of a perutah remained of it. But if four fifths of a perutah remained, when he eats against it he must add a fifth of a perutah for the fifth (which is a quarter of the principal, as above, 5:1), so together with the fifth it is worth a whole perutah and it does not become ordinary (and see above, 5:4 that a fifth not worth a perutah is not added, but that case speaks of a maaser that was originally worth that much, whereas here the maaser was originally worth a dinar; Arukh HaShulchan 134:16).

whenever the pure eat and drink, this sela is deconsecrated onto it. The deconsecration takes effect when the pure people take food from the common bowl or pour into their cup from the common jug (Rik"u, Kesef Mishneh, and others).

neta revai. The fruit of a tree in the fourth year of its planting (in the first three years the fruit is called orlah and is forbidden for eating and benefit. And although many laws of neta revai depend on the laws of orlah, the Rambam put the laws of neta revai before the laws of orlah, which will be explained in the next chapter, because of the similarity between neta revai and maaser sheni in the laws of eating and redemption).
and its law is to be eaten by its owners in Jerusalem like maaser sheni. According to the laws of eating stated for maaser sheni (above, chapters 2-3).
and just as there is no maaser sheni in Syria. Above, 1:14.
so there is no neta revai in Syria. And all the more so outside the Land, but in the Land it applies even after the destruction (Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 10:15).

for you have no sacred item whose law was not specified in the Torah as to whom it belongs, except for neta revai. The Torah specified to whom every sacred item is given except neta revai, so we must say that the verse "and each man's sacred items shall be his" refers to neta revai.
redeems as with maaser sheni, and if he redeemed it for himself, he adds a fifth. The laws of redemption and of adding the fifth were detailed above, chapters 4-5.
to the season of the tithes. The stage of growth at which produce becomes obligated in terumot and ma'asrot (see Hilchot Maaser 2:3-5).
until it becomes grain. A fruit that is fit for eating.
